title: Output-sensitive convex hull complexity
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\geq4\), determine up to constant factors the optimal deterministic output-sensitive running time for constructing the convex hull of \(n\geq d+1\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\) in general position, as a function of \(n\) and the actual number \(f\) of hull facets. The coordinate array is the input. Output the complete facial structure of the hull, as specified below. The required complexity must cover every realizable pair \((n,f)\), including small hulls, and retain logarithmic factors.
why: Sharp output-sensitive hull bounds would connect the work of discovering a geometric boundary to its actual combinatorial size. This matters for hull construction, polyhedral representations and geometric computations whose input contains many nonextreme points.
status_note: The complexity question is open in the primary source and problem entry. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no matching characterization for the stated higher-dimensional family. The displayed general-dimensional bound is attributed to 1996 rather than presented as a verified current record.

progress.text: Chan obtains output-sensitive upper bounds in every fixed dimension under general position.
The Open Problems Project records the unresolved optimal output-sensitive complexity.
The ESA paper establishes a refined planar universal-optimality result, for a different dimensional and output setting.

importance.reason: A fundamental input/output tradeoff in higher-dimensional geometry; it asks whether the work needed to find a hull can be matched to its actual facial complexity.

sentences: An output-sensitive convex hull algorithm charges for both its input points and the facets it actually produces.
The question asks for the best such running time for point sets in fixed-dimensional Euclidean space.
Small hulls should be cheaper than the worst-case hull complexity would suggest.
The difficult target is to reconcile reading the input, identifying extreme structure, and listing the output with nearly optimal overhead.
Progress would improve geometric optimization whenever many input points contribute little to the final convex boundary.

definitions: General position means every subset of at most \(d+1\) input points is affinely independent. The convex hull is \(H=\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i p_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\). Its proper nonempty faces are intersections with supporting hyperplanes; a facet has dimension \(d-1\). The promise makes \(H\) full-dimensional and simplicial, with exactly \(d\) vertices per facet. Output each proper nonempty face by its set of input-vertex indices and list every containment incidence between faces of consecutive dimensions; also identify the facets. The total output size is \(O_d(f)\). Interior input points need not be output. Let \(\mathcal D_d\) be the pairs \((n,f)\) realized by a valid input, and let \(T_A(n,f)\) be the supremum of algorithm \(A\)’s steps over all such inputs with exactly these parameters. One finite deterministic program per fixed \(d\) must work for all \(n\); it is given neither \(f\) nor advice. The model has exact real registers with rational program constants and indexed memory; \(+,-,\times,/\), comparisons, copies and memory accesses cost one each. Integer indices and counters have \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits at time \(t\), with ordinary word arithmetic and comparisons charged. No floor, extraction of real digits, or free geometric query is available. Reading input and reporting faces are charged. Coordinates have no bounded-precision promise, and no randomization or input distribution is used.
answer_criterion: Provide a noncircular positive rate \(g_d(n,f)\) on each domain \(\mathcal D_d\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds. For each fixed \(d\geq4\), give one uniform algorithm \(A_d\) with \(T_{A_d}(n,f)\leq C_dg_d(n,f)\) on all feasible pairs with sufficiently large \(n\). For every correct algorithm \(A\), prove \(T_A(n,f)\geq c_{A,d}g_d(n,f)\) on all feasible pairs with sufficiently large \(n\). Positive constants and thresholds may depend on \(d\), and in the lower bound on \(A\), but not on the feasible pair. A worst-case bound in \(n\) alone, listing only extreme vertices, or resolving only dimensions two and three is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The Open Problems Project asks for the best output-sensitive hull algorithm. The general-position convention used here is explicit in Chan’s cited primary paper. Without it, a facet can contain many vertices, and the number of facets alone need not measure the amount of output.

Output sensitivity accounts for what the particular input produces. Many points may lie inside a hull with few facets, so a bound based solely on the largest possible hull of an equally large point set can greatly exceed the size of the actual result.

Chan’s 1996 theorem gives \(O_d(n\log f+(nf)^{1-1/(\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1)}\log^{O_d(1)}n)\) time. The paper contrasts this with the \(\Omega_d(n\log f+f)\) lower bound and explains the range of small outputs where its upper bound is optimal. These are dated results, not a claim that every intervening bound has been exhaustively surveyed.

The same paper distinguishes the hull’s full facial structure from the task of finding only its extreme points, and records optimal \(O(n\log f)\) algorithms in dimensions two and three. In dimension four there are also stronger specialized bounds than a literal use of the general-dimensional expression.

The ESA 2025 work on universal optimality concerns planar hulls and additionally reports certificates for interior points. It addresses a refined form of input sensitivity but does not settle the higher-dimensional two-parameter target here.

The fixed dimension is allowed to affect constants; the input size and output size are not. General position is a substantive source assumption, not a license to perturb a degenerate input while pretending its output size remains unchanged.
